meta.title: The Great Mortality
meta.curriculum: Tennessee Grade 7 Social Studies, Middle Ages in Western Europe (7.27–7.39); links back to East Asia / Mongols (7.01–7.11)
meta.markup: Inline Codex terms use [[term-id]] or [[term-id|display text]]. Rendering one marks the term as seen. {town}, {steward}, {month} are placeholders.

decrees.name: Hold ships offshore forty days
decrees.description: Let no galley touch the quay till the moon turns.
decrees.truth: Works. Blocks most infected ships (8% leak). Lowers port tolls. Unrest +3 on issue, +2/month.

decrees.name: Close the port
decrees.description: Chain the harbor. The merchants will howl.
decrees.truth: Works best against the sea route. No tolls. Unrest +6 on issue, +8/month (hunger).

decrees.name: Seal a town's roads
decrees.description: Set guards on every road. None in, none out.
decrees.truth: Works. Closes every road and footpath touching the town. Halves its tithes. Unrest +3 on issue, +3/month per sealed town.

decrees.name: Clean the streets and granaries
decrees.description: Sweep the filth and burn the spoiled grain.
decrees.truth: Helps, for the wrong reason: fewer rats near people. Kills 15% of the town's rats and dampens rat spread 10% for the rest of the run.

decrees.name: Burn herbs to cleanse the air
decrees.description: Rosemary and juniper against the foul vapors.
decrees.truth: Does nothing to the plague. Unrest -2. Can trigger the herb-fires clue.

decrees.name: Hire physicians
decrees.description: Learned men of Salerno, with vinegar and lancets.
decrees.truth: Does nothing to deaths. Unrest -5. First use earns the beaked-mask card.

decrees.name: Hold a procession
decrees.description: Carry the relics through the streets and pray.
decrees.truth: Backfires. Unrest -8, but crowds multiply person-to-person spread (x1.8) in that town for the month.

decrees.name: Close the bathhouses
decrees.description: Open pores let the sickness in, the doctors say.
decrees.truth: Does nothing. Unrest +4. Earns the bathing card.

decrees.name: Flee to the countryside
decrees.description: Ends your stewardship. Asks you twice.
decrees.truth: Ends the run as 'the Fled'. Remaining months auto-play with all toggles left as they were.

opening.label: Messina · October 1347
narration: Twelve galleys from the Black Sea.
Half the crews are dead at their oars.
The harbor master will not let them land.
By morning, they have landed anyway.
Driven from Messina, the galleys row north along the coast. Toward your port.

titleCard.title: Something is killing your people. Find out what.
titleCard.body: You are the [[steward]] of six towns on the Italian coast. Choose your name.

quietReportLines: The month turned without word from the roads.
Markets opened and bells rang, for ordinary reasons.
Nothing came to the ledger but weather and work.
The towns kept their own counsel this month.

early: The air itself has turned. Foul [[miasma]] rises from the marshes and the earth's cracks. Burn sweet herbs and we may yet clean it.
Your blood is a balance of four [[humors]]. Keep it cool and calm, avoid hot baths that open the skin, and the poison finds no door.
spreading: I have read Galen and Avicenna on this. Bad air settles in low, damp places. Keep the windows shut against the south wind.
winter: The cold air is cleaner. You see? The deaths are fewer. The vapors sink in winter.

early: Many believe this sickness is a judgment for our sins. Let the people gather and pray together. They need hope as much as bread.
spreading: I have buried more in a week than in all my years before. Let us carry the relics through the streets, so no one feels abandoned.
In the north, bands of [[flagellants]] march from town to town, whipping themselves in penance. His Holiness does not approve of them. I pray we never see them here.
winter: The deaths have slowed. Perhaps heaven has heard us. I will keep praying, and so should you.

early: In March of 1345, Saturn, Jupiter and Mars met in Aquarius. The great doctors of Paris say that [[conjunction]] poisoned the air. We are living under its shadow.
spreading: The stars move slowly, my lord. What they set in motion will run its course. Burn herbs at the hour of Venus; it is the best we can do.
winter: See how the planets drift apart in winter. Their poison weakens.

early: Every day the galleys sit at anchor, we lose a thousand [[florin|florins]]. The city lives on that harbor, my lord.
Sicily is a long way off. Sickness in Messina is no reason to starve Portoreale.
spreading: People are hungry. Grain rots in the holds out there. Open the harbor before the city opens it for you.
winter: Trade is slow in winter anyway. If you must hold the ships, now is cheapest. But spring will come.

theories.text: From foul air rising from swamps and earthquakes
From the East, by sea, on the galleys from Caffa

questions.notYetHint: You know where the galleys came from. Now prove the sickness came with them.
questions.solvedSummary: It came from the East along the trade routes, and reached Italy on Genoese galleys from [[caffa|Caffa]].

theories.text: As a judgment, wherever it wills

questions.notYetHint: One clue points this way. Find a second.
questions.solvedSummary: It travels with people and their goods: ships, carts, cloth and grain. Stop the movement and you slow the sickness.

theories.text: Something tiny that lives on rats, and on people

questions.notYetHint: Watch the [[granary|granaries]]. Something dies there before people do.
questions.solvedSummary: Fleas. They live on rats, and probably on people too. When the rats die, the fleas look for new hosts.

questions.text: Why does it slow down in winter, but not always?

theories.text: Heaven shows mercy in the cold
Cold air is clean air, so winter is always safe
The planets drift apart in winter
Cold slows its tiny carriers, but a lung form spreads by coughing

questions.notYetHint: You have seen half the pattern. Watch a winter closely.
questions.solvedSummary: Fleas slow down in the cold, so [[bubonic-plague|bubonic plague]] eases in winter. But [[pneumonic-plague|pneumonic plague]] lives in the lungs and spreads by coughing, cold or not.

notYet.text: You may be right, but an investigator needs more proof.

wrong.religiousText: Many people believed this sincerely. Your evidence shows how it spread:
wrong.noClueText: None of your clues supports this yet. Keep watching the months.

clues.title: Galleys from the East
clues.text: The sick crews came from [[caffa|Caffa]] on the Black Sea.

clues.title: The quarantined galley
clues.text: The crew died aboard at anchor, and the town stayed healthy. The [[quarantine]] held.
clues.trigger: An infected ship arrives while ships are held, and the port has no new cases that month.
clues.reportText: A galley held at anchor flew the black flag. By month's end its crew were dead aboard. Portoreale had no new sick.

clues.title: The village with no road
clues.text: Fontenera is untouched, under the same sky and the same air.
clues.trigger: Month 5 or later, Fontenera has no burials, and at least 3 towns do.
clues.reportText: Fontenera, reached only by a goat path, has buried no one. The same wind blows there.

clues.title: The herb fires failed
clues.text: Rosemary and juniper burned for a month in {town}. The sick kept coming.
clues.trigger: Herbs were burned in a town, and its new cases next month were no lower.
clues.reportText: The herb fires in {town} burned all month. The sick did not slow.

clues.title: Dead rats in the granary
clues.text: In {town}, the rats died first. People fell sick after.
clues.trigger: A town's rats die off visibly before its first burial.
clues.reportText: The keeper of the [[granary]] in {town} swept out dead rats by the basket. No one is sick there. Yet.

clues.title: The ragman's cart
clues.text: Clothes from a dead household were sold in {town}. The sickness followed the cart.
clues.trigger: Ragman event moves cloth from a ravaged town to a healthy neighbor, and an outbreak follows within 2 months.
clues.reportText: A ragman sold the bedding of the dead in {town}. Within weeks, {town} was burying its own.

clues.title: The grain ship
clues.text: Not one sailor aboard was sick. But after its sacks were unloaded, the sickness came to {town}.
clues.trigger: A grain ship with a healthy crew docks at an open port, and an outbreak follows within 2 months.
clues.reportText: A grain ship unloaded at the quay with a healthy crew. Weeks later, the sickness was in {town}.

clues.title: The winter lull
clues.text: In the coldest months, the swollen-gland sickness slowed.
clues.trigger: In Dec–Feb, regional new cases fall at least 30% below the autumn peak (peak must exceed 50).
clues.reportText: The frost came, and the bell for the dead rang less often.

clues.title: The coughing sickness
clues.text: In winter, a form that spat blood spread fast in {town}, from person to person.
clues.trigger: In Dec–Feb, a town has more than 3 people sick with the pneumonic form in a week.
clues.reportText: In {town}, a new and quicker form: the sick cough blood and die in two days. Those who nurse them follow.

lensReveal.title: The Physician's Lens
lensReveal.body: You have found what no one in 1348 could see. Now look at your region as it truly was.
lensReveal.footnote: The Lens stays unsealed in every game from now on.

legend.title: Rat colonies
legend.text: Every town had rats. When plague swept through them, they died, and their fleas went looking for new hosts.

legend.title: Flea spread
legend.text: Fleas rode in grain sacks, cloth and clothing, on rats and on people. That is how the sickness traveled with goods.

legend.title: Bubonic vs. pneumonic
legend.text: Bubonic plague came from flea bites and slowed in the cold. Pneumonic plague infected the lungs and spread by coughing, in any weather.

legend.title: Why Fontenera was spared
legend.text: No road, little trade, few strangers. Isolation protected it, not cleaner air.

codex.meaning: The person who runs a region on behalf of its lord: collecting taxes, keeping order, giving commands. That's you.
codex.why: In 1348, decisions like yours were made by real stewards, councils and lords, with no idea what was really killing people.

codex.meaning: A long, narrow ship moved by oars and sails. Italian merchants used galleys to carry goods across the Mediterranean and Black Sea.
codex.why: Galleys were fast and carried rats, fleas and sick sailors from port to port. They brought the plague to Italy.

codex.meaning: A deadly disease that spreads widely. In 1348, people mostly called the plague 'the pestilence' or 'the great mortality.'
codex.why: The name 'Black Death' came centuries later. Knowing what people called it helps you read the real sources.
codex.then: A punishment, a poison in the air, or both.
codex.now: An old word for any widespread deadly disease.

codex.meaning: Bad air. Doctors believed disease came from foul vapors rising from swamps, rotting things, or cracks in the earth.
codex.why: Many decrees in this game are based on miasma. Watch which ones actually help.
codex.then: The leading medical explanation for plague.
codex.now: Wrong. Most diseases come from germs: bacteria and viruses. Bad smells aren't the cause.

codex.pos: noun · from the Italian quaranta, forty
codex.meaning: Keeping ships, goods or people apart from everyone else for a set time, to see whether sickness shows itself before they come in.
codex.why: Your "hold ships offshore" decree is this idea, thirty years before anyone wrote it into law.
codex.then: Ragusa held arrivals thirty days on an island; Venice later made it forty.
codex.now: Still used. The length is set by how long a disease takes to show, not by the number forty.

codex.meaning: The most common form of the Black Death. It caused painful swellings called buboes in the neck, armpits and groin. It spread mainly through flea bites.
codex.why: Because fleas slow down in cold weather, bubonic plague eased in winter. That's a clue.
codex.then: Doctors thought buboes were poison collecting in the body.
codex.now: Buboes are swollen lymph nodes fighting the infection. Antibiotics cure it if given early.

codex.meaning: A form of plague in the lungs. The sick coughed, and the coughing spread it directly to the people around them.
codex.why: It didn't need fleas, so cold weather didn't stop it. It was even deadlier than bubonic plague.

codex.meaning: Someone blamed for something they did not do, often because people are afraid and want someone to blame.
codex.why: During the plague, Jewish communities were falsely blamed and attacked. Learning the word helps you spot the pattern, then and now.

codex.meaning: A building where a town stored its grain for the year.
codex.why: Grain attracts rats. Granaries are where people first saw rats dying, though no one understood what it meant.

codex.meaning: When planets appear close together in the sky. Saturn, Jupiter and Mars had a conjunction in March 1345.
codex.why: The top doctors in Paris officially blamed the plague on this conjunction in 1348. It shows that even experts can be confidently wrong.
codex.then: Planets could poison the air on Earth.
codex.now: Planets have no effect on disease. A conjunction is just a line-of-sight coincidence.

codex.meaning: The pope from 1342 to 1352, who lived in Avignon, France, during the Black Death.
codex.why: In 1348 he declared that Jews were not to blame and ordered them protected. He also condemned the flagellants.

codex.meaning: The tiny bacterium that causes plague. It was discovered in 1894 and named after Alexandre Yersin.
codex.why: It's the real answer to the mystery that no one in 1348 could solve.

codex.meaning: A trading city on the Crimean coast of the Black Sea, run by merchants from Genoa. Today it's called Feodosia.
codex.why: The plague broke out there during a Mongol siege in 1346, and galleys fleeing Caffa carried it toward Italy.

codex.meaning: A powerful Italian city-state and sea-trading power, with trading posts all the way to the Black Sea.
codex.why: Genoese ships linked Italy to the trade routes from Asia, and that is how the plague arrived.

codex.meaning: Trade routes across Asia linking China to the Black Sea and Mediterranean. Silk, spices, ideas and religions traveled along them.
codex.why: Disease traveled the same roads. The more connected the world, the faster a sickness could spread.

codex.meaning: The huge empire founded by Genghis Khan in the 1200s, stretching from China to Eastern Europe.
codex.why: By connecting so much of Asia, the Mongols made trade easier. That connection also helped the plague move west. You may have studied them in your East Asia unit.

codex.meaning: The ancient belief that the body had four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Health meant keeping them in balance.
codex.why: Medieval doctors treated plague by bleeding patients and changing diets to rebalance the humors. It didn't work.
codex.now: Wrong, though it shaped medicine for almost 2,000 years.

codex.meaning: A quarantine hospital, often on an island, where travelers and sick people were kept apart from a city.
codex.why: Venice built the first permanent one in 1423. It turned quarantine from an emergency order into something a city planned for.
codex.then: An island where ships' crews waited out forty days.
codex.now: Modern quarantine stations exist at airports and borders.

codex.meaning: Groups who marched from town to town whipping themselves, believing their suffering would make God end the plague.
codex.why: Their marches drew crowds and spread fear. Pope Clement VI condemned them in 1349.

codex.meaning: A peasant bound to a lord's land. Serfs farmed the land and owed the lord work and payments, and couldn't simply leave.
codex.why: After the plague killed so many workers, surviving serfs had new power to demand better treatment.

codex.meaning: The system of medieval Europe where lords held land, peasants worked it, and everyone owed duties to someone above them.
codex.why: Feudalism depended on lots of cheap labor. The plague took that away, and the system began to break down.

codex.meaning: A disease spreading quickly to many people in one area at the same time.
codex.why: Each town in your region has its own epidemic. Together, across a continent, they become something bigger.

codex.meaning: An epidemic that spreads across several countries or continents.
codex.why: The Black Death was one of the deadliest pandemics in human history.
codex.then: No word for it. People only knew the sickness was everywhere.
codex.now: Public health systems track pandemics around the world.

codex.meaning: A gold coin first minted in Florence in 1252. It was trusted across Europe, a bit like the dollar today.
codex.why: Your treasury is counted in florins. Every decree has a cost, just as real ones did.

chronicles.title: Ships from Caffa
chronicles.body:
No one in 1347 knew where the sickness began. Today, scientists who study ancient DNA and old gravestones think it started in Central Asia in the late 1330s. From there it moved along the trade routes that the [[mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]] had joined together, the same [[silk-road|Silk Road]] that carried silk, spices and ideas between China and Europe.

In 1346 a Mongol army besieged [[caffa|Caffa]], a trading city on the Black Sea run by merchants from [[genoa|Genoa]]. The sickness broke out among the soldiers, then inside the walls. A famous story says the attackers threw bodies over the walls. Historians aren't sure it happened, and rats could easily have carried the sickness in.

Genoese [[galley|galleys]] sailed for home and took the sickness with them. In October 1347 they reached Messina, in Sicily. Within a year it was everywhere in Italy.
remember: The plague traveled along trade routes from Central Asia to Europe.
Genoese ships brought it to Sicily in October 1347.
The routes that spread goods and ideas also spread disease.

quiz.q: How did the plague reach Italy?
options: On the wind over the Alps
With a Mongol army that invaded Italy
quiz.explain: Galleys fleeing Caffa carried it to Messina in 1347.

quiz.q: Why did the Mongol Empire matter to the plague's spread?
options: Its trade routes connected Asia and Europe
It closed all trade with Europe
quiz.explain: A connected world moved goods quickly, and disease with them.

chronicles.title: Fear and Blame
chronicles.body:
When the sickness came and no one could say why, people looked for someone to blame. In towns across Europe, frightened neighbors accused Jewish families of poisoning the wells. It was false. Jewish families drank from the same wells and died of the same sickness. But fear does not wait for proof.

In many places the accusations led to terrible violence. In some, leaders refused to allow it. In 1348 [[pope-clement-vi|Pope Clement VI]] declared the accusations false and ordered that Jewish people be protected, pointing out that the plague struck places with no Jewish community at all.

In your region, the steward stood at the gate. The record says simply: no one was harmed.
remember: A [[scapegoat]] is someone blamed for a thing they did not do.
Fear plus ignorance is dangerous. Evidence is the cure for both.
Some leaders protected people. Leadership is a choice.

options: A person who caused a problem
Someone blamed for something they didn't do
A goat used in religious ceremonies today
quiz.explain: Scapegoats are blamed unfairly, often because people are afraid.

quiz.q: What evidence did Pope Clement VI point to?
options: Jewish communities caught the plague less
The plague struck places with no Jewish community at all
quiz.explain: If the plague came where no Jewish people lived, they couldn't be the cause. He also noted that Jewish families died of it too.

chronicles.title: The Great Mortality
chronicles.body:
Between 1347 and 1351 the [[pestilence]] swept across Europe, from Italy to England, Scandinavia and the edge of Russia. Historians estimate it killed between a third and half of Europe's people, perhaps 25 to 50 million. Crowded cities suffered most. Florence may have lost more than half its people. In Siena, work stopped on a giant new cathedral, and its unfinished walls still stand.

Then came the surprising part. With so many dead, there weren't enough workers. Surviving [[serf|serfs]] and laborers could demand higher wages or leave for towns that paid more. Lords tried to stop them. England passed the Statute of Labourers in 1351 to freeze wages. But the old [[feudalism|feudal]] order had begun to crack.

The plague did not leave for good. It returned every ten or twenty years for three centuries. It was not one [[epidemic]] but a [[pandemic]] that kept coming back.
remember: The Black Death killed roughly a third to half of Europe's people between 1347 and 1351.
The worker shortage gave peasants more power and weakened feudalism.
The plague returned again and again for about 300 years.

quiz.q: About how much of Europe's population died?
options: Between a third and a half
quiz.explain: Estimates range from about 30% to 50%, more in some cities.

quiz.q: Why did the plague weaken feudalism?
options: With fewer workers, peasants could demand better pay and freedom
quiz.explain: Labor became scarce and valuable, so the old system of bound serfs began to break down.

chronicles.title: Forty Days
chronicles.body:
On 27 July 1377, the city of Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik in Croatia, passed a new law. Anyone arriving from a place with plague had to wait thirty days on a nearby island or in a nearby town before entering the city. It's the oldest known [[quarantine]] law, and the document still survives.

Other cities copied the idea, and the waiting time grew to forty days: quaranta giorni in Italian. That's where our word comes from. Why forty? No one knows for sure. Forty was an important number in religion and in old medical writings about illness.

In 1423 Venice built the first permanent [[lazaretto]], a quarantine hospital on an island in its lagoon.

Notice what quarantine did not need: no one had to know about germs. People only had to notice that the sickness arrived with travelers. That's exactly what you've been investigating.
remember: Ragusa wrote the first known quarantine law in 1377.
'Quarantine' comes from the Italian for forty days.
It worked by careful observation, long before anyone understood germs.

quiz.q: Where does the word 'quarantine' come from?
options: The name of a Venetian doctor

quiz.q: How could quarantine work before anyone knew about germs?
options: People observed that sickness arrived with travelers
The planets showed when to use it
quiz.explain: Observation and evidence were enough, even without the full explanation.

chronicles.title: The Answer: Yersin and Simond
chronicles.body:
For more than 500 years, no one knew what caused the plague. Then in 1894 a new outbreak reached Hong Kong, and two scientists raced to find the cause: Alexandre Yersin of the Pasteur Institute in Paris, and Kitasato Shibasaburō of Japan. Yersin found a tiny bacterium in the swollen glands of victims. It was later named [[yersinia-pestis|Yersinia pestis]] in his honor.

In 1898, Paul-Louis Simond showed how it reached people. When infected rats died, their fleas jumped to new hosts, including humans.

In 2011, scientists found the bacterium's DNA in the teeth of people buried in a London plague cemetery from 1348 and 1349. That proved this was the cause of the Black Death. Some researchers now think fleas and lice on people spread it between humans too.

Today plague still exists, but antibiotics can cure it if it's treated quickly.
remember: The bacterium Yersinia pestis causes plague.
Fleas carried it from rats to people, and probably between people too.
DNA from 1348 graves confirmed it caused the Black Death.

quiz.explain: Yersinia pestis, spread mostly by flea bites, and by coughing in the pneumonic form.

quiz.q: How did scientists confirm what caused the Black Death?
options: They found the bacterium's DNA in skeletons from 1348–49
quiz.explain: Ancient DNA from plague cemeteries gave direct proof.

timeline.note: the sickness returns every ten or twenty years for three centuries

cards.myth: Plague doctors wore beaked masks in 1348
cards.story: The famous bird-beaked costume dates from the 1600s, almost 300 years after the Black Death. In 1348, doctors wore ordinary robes.
cards.howWeKnow: The earliest descriptions and prints of the costume are from the 1600s. Nothing like it appears in images from the 1300s.
cards.caption: Earned in {month}, for hiring physicians.

cards.story: People in 1348 called it the great mortality, the great pestilence, or simply the plague. 'Black Death' came into wide use centuries later.
cards.howWeKnow: Writers from the 1340s, like Boccaccio, never use the name. It became popular in English in the 1800s.
cards.caption: Earned at the end of your first stewardship.

cards.myth: "Ring Around the Rosie" is about the plague
cards.story: It's a fun story, but folklorists say no. The rhyme wasn't printed until 1881, and the plague explanation only appeared in the 1900s. Older versions don't even have the sneezing or falling down.
cards.howWeKnow: Folklorists traced the printed versions and found no plague link before the 20th century.
cards.caption: Earned in {month}, when {town} buried its last.

cards.story: Medieval towns had public bathhouses, and many people used them. During the plague some closed, because doctors feared that warm water opened the skin's pores to bad air.
cards.howWeKnow: Town records list bathhouses and their rules, and plague advice from doctors warns against hot baths.
cards.caption: Earned in {month}, for closing the bathhouses.

cards.story: Rats mattered: their fleas carried the bacterium. But some scientists now think human fleas and body lice spread much of it from person to person, and the lung form spread by coughing. Scientists still debate how much each mattered.
cards.howWeKnow: A 2018 study compared death patterns in nine European cities and found person-to-person spread fit better than rats alone.
cards.caption: Earned for solving Question III.

cards.story: Many people did. But in 1348 the top doctors of Paris officially blamed a planetary conjunction from 1345. Others blamed bad air, earthquakes, or falsely blamed their neighbors.
cards.howWeKnow: The Paris doctors' written report to the King of France survives.
cards.caption: Earned in {month}, when the astrologer first spoke.

cards.story: The first quarantine law was written in Ragusa (today's Dubrovnik) in 1377. Ships waited thirty days on a nearby island. Venice stretched it to forty: quaranta giorni.
cards.howWeKnow: The law survives in Ragusa's city archive, dated 27 July 1377.
cards.caption: Earned in {month}, for holding a galley forty days.

cards.story: Plague still lives in wild rodents and their fleas on several continents, including the western United States. A few people catch it each year, but antibiotics cure it if treated early.
cards.howWeKnow: Health agencies like the CDC track every case. The U.S. averages about seven a year.
cards.caption: Earned for unsealing the Physician's Lens.

list.name: the Wise
list.rule: Survival >= 75% and at least 6 town-months of quarantine (ships held + port closed + roads sealed)
list.citation: who {actions}, and so was hated for a season and thanked for a lifetime.

list.name: the Iron Gate
list.rule: Port closed 12 or more of 18 months
list.citation: who chained the harbor and kept it chained, though the city went hungry.

list.name: the Merchant Prince
list.rule: Port never held or closed, treasury ended above its start, and survival >= 60%
list.citation: who kept the harbor open and the florins flowing, and gambled, and won.

list.name: the Devout
list.citation: who {actions}, and never let the people pray alone.

list.name: the Steady
list.rule: Unrest never above 50 and survival >= 60% (also the fallback when survival >= 60%)
list.citation: who {actions}, and kept the peace when all around was fear.

list.name: the Unlucky
list.citation: who {actions}, and still the bells did not stop.

list.name: the Fled
list.citation: who left for the hills before dawn, as many did.

list.name: the Overthrown
list.citation: who could not hold the city's trust, and lost it.

actionPhrases.processions: carried the relics through the streets

epithets.actionPhraseRule: Use the two most-used actions this run (by months active or count), joined with 'and'. If none, use 'none'.

scriptedEvents.title: A crowd at the well
paragraphs: Word reaches you before dawn. A crowd has gathered at the old well in the lower town. They say the water has been poisoned. They say they know who did it: their Jewish neighbors, the dyers and the bookbinder's family on the Via dei Tintori.
It is not true. The Via dei Tintori drinks from the same well, and buries its dead in the same month as everyone else. But fear does not wait for proof.
scriptedEvents.stewardAction: You go yourself, with the guard. You stand at the gate of the Via dei Tintori until the crowd goes home. No one is harmed. In the morning you post a decree: whoever harms a neighbor over this answers to the steward.
scriptedEvents.footer: Unrest rises a little. A chronicle has been added: Fear and Blame. A word has been added to your Codex: [[scapegoat]].

reportLines.held-ship-leak: A galley slipped its anchor in the night and tied up at the quay before the guard could stop it.
reportLines.overland-arrival: Travelers on the inland road reached Santa Lucia, coughing and feverish.
reportLines.ragman: A ragman's cart left {from} for {to}, loaded with the bedding of the dead.
reportLines.income: Treasury took {income} [[florin|florins]] in tolls and tithes.

overthrown.title: {steward} the Overthrown
overthrown.body: The council met without you. By evening the guard had changed sides, and by morning there was a new steward. The sickness did not notice.
overthrown.footnote: What you learned stays learned. The Evidence Board remembers.

fled.title: {steward} the Fled
fled.body: You left for the hills before dawn with your household and what the mules could carry. Boccaccio's ten young Florentines did the same, and told a hundred stories over ten days. The towns went on without you.
fled.footnote: A new chronicle has opened: The Great Mortality.
